q: 1. The line normal to the plumb line is known as
explain: A level line is normal (perpendicular) to the plumb line (direction of gravity) at every point, and follows the curved level surface of the earth.

q: 2. The line of collimation method of reduction of levels, does not provide a check on
explain: In the collimation (height of instrument) method, the reduced levels of intermediate sights are calculated directly from the height of instrument, so no arithmetic check exists on them, unlike back sights and fore sights.

q: 3. A back sight indicates the ... of the instrument
explain: A back sight (BS), taken on a point of known elevation, is used to determine the height of the instrument (HI) above the datum.

q: 4. Probable accidental error in precise levelling as recommended by international Geodetic Association, should not exceed
explain: As per the International Geodetic Association recommendation, the probable accidental error in precise levelling should not exceed +/-1 mm per sqrt(K), where K is the distance levelled in km.

q: 5. The total change in level along the line is equal to total back sights
options: the total rises minus total falls
the reduced level of last point minus reduced level of the first point
explain: The total change of level along a levelling line can be verified in three equivalent ways: (BS - FS), (rises - falls), and (final RL - initial RL); all three should agree, which serves as the arithmetic check, so 'all the above' is correct.

q: 6. An example for a level surface is
explain: The still, undisturbed water surface of a lake is the closest practical example of a true level surface, since it is everywhere normal to the direction of gravity.

q: 7. Level line and horizontal line are
explain: A level (curved) line and a horizontal (tangential straight) line coincide closely for short distances, but diverge for longer distances due to the earth's curvature.

q: 8. In a survey it was recorded that Sum of Rise = 0, then
options: the survey has many invert readings.
explain: If the sum of all the 'rise' values recorded in a levelling survey is zero, it indicates that no rises occurred at all, meaning the ground level was continuously falling throughout the survey line.

q: 9. Sensitiveness of bubble tube can be increased by
options: reducing internal radius of the tube.
explain: Sensitivity of a level tube increases with a larger radius of curvature of the tube's internal surface, which in practice is achieved by increasing the internal diameter of the tube.

q: 10. The surface of zero elevation around the earth, which is slightly irregular and curved is known as
explain: The geoid is the theoretical surface of the Earth's oceans if they were at rest, serving as the global reference for elevations.

q: 11. When the bubble of the level tube of level, remains central
options: axis of the telescope is horizontal
geometrical axis of the telescope is horizontal
explain: When the bubble is centred (in an adjusted level), the axis of the bubble tube is horizontal, which in turn means the line of sight is horizontal.

q: 12. In an internal focussing type of telescope, the negative lens provided is
explain: Internal focusing telescopes use a movable double concave (negative) lens located between the objective and the diaphragm.

q: 13. The errors in levelling due to earths' curvature are
explain: The error introduced by the earth's curvature, if uncorrected, always makes the staff reading appear too great (object appears lower than actual), which is treated as a positive error in the observed reading.

q: 14. The combined correction for refraction and earth's curvature (in levelling observations) is
explain: The standard formula for combined correction for curvature and refraction (distance d in km) is 0.06735*d2 metres, obtained after applying the standard refraction coefficient to the pure curvature correction of 0.0785*d2.

q: 15. In a constant level tube, size of the bubble remains constant because upper wall of tube has
explain: A large radius of curvature in the upper wall allows for a more sensitive and stable bubble length despite minor temperature changes.

q: 16. Height of instrument method of levelling as compared to rise and fall method is
explain: While less accurate in terms of self-checking intermediate sights, the HI method is significantly faster and easier to calculate.

q: 17. The rise and fall method
options: provides a check on the intermediate readings
is preferable for differential and check levelling
explain: Due to its rigorous checking of all staff readings, it is the preferred method for high-precision engineering surveys.

q: 18. The sensitivity of bubble tube can be increased by
options: decreasing the radius of curvature of tube
explain: Note: increasing the radius of curvature of the bubble tube generally increases sensitivity in standard theory; however, per the book's printed answer key, decreasing the radius of curvature is given as the answer here - please verify against your copy.

q: 19. With the rise of temperature, the sensitivity of bubble tube
explain: As temperature rises, the liquid inside the bubble tube becomes less viscous and the bubble itself expands, generally reducing the precision/sensitivity of readings, so sensitivity decreases.

q: 20. While doing leveling in undulating terrain, it is preferable to set level on
explain: In undulating terrain, setting the level instrument on one side of the slope (rather than at the very top or bottom) often provides better command over multiple staff points with fewer instrument setups.

q: 21. The telescope of a dumpy level
options: is rigidly fixed to the leveling head
can be tilted in a vertical plane
can be taken out of its supports and reversed
permits interchange of eye piece and object glass
explain: In a dumpy level, the telescope is rigidly and permanently fixed to the vertical spindle/leveling head, distinguishing it from tilting or reversible levels.

q: 22. The reciprocal levelling eliminates
options: the error due to curvature and refraction
explain: By taking readings from both ends of the line, reciprocal leveling cancels out the combined effects of curvature, refraction, and any residual collimation error.

q: 23. A fixed point of reference of known elevation is called
explain: A bench mark is, by definition, a fixed point of reference whose elevation is already known and used to start/check levelling operations.

q: 24. The height of instrument is equal to
options: reduced level of bench mark + back sight
reduced level of bench mark + fore sight
reduced level of bench mark + intermediate sight
explain: The height of the instrument (H.I.) is calculated by adding the back sight reading to the reduced level of the point on which the back sight was taken (typically a bench mark).

q: 25. The first reading taken at turning point is
explain: At a turning point (change point), a Fore Sight is taken to find the point's elevation, and then the first reading after moving the instrument is a Back Sight to continue the line.

q: 26. A method of differential levelling is used in order to find the difference in elevation between two points when
options: the difference in elevation between them is too great
explain: Differential levelling using a series of intermediate instrument setups is used whenever the two points are too far apart, have obstacles between them, or have too great a difference in elevation to be observed in a single setup -- so all these conditions apply.

q: 27. Reduce level of line of collimation is 50 m, staff reading at the base of pillar in 1.15 m then find the reduce level of base of pillar
explain: RL of point = RL of Collimation (HI) - Staff Reading = 50 - 1.15 = 48.85 m.

q: 28. The Bench Mark of a point is 400m. Back sight reading at bench mark is 2.20 and fore sight reading of point A is 2.10 then find the RL of the point A
29. In leveling across a hill, the level should be set up on
explain: When leveling up or down a slope, the instrument is placed on the side of the hill in a 'zigzag' pattern to maintain a manageable staff height.

q: 30. The curvature and refraction corrections applied to staff readings respectively are
explain: Curvature correction is negative (subtractive) while refraction correction is positive (additive) to the staff reading.

q: 31. Fifteen readings were recorded in a level field book. If the instrument was shifted after 5th, 10th and 15th readings, then the fore sights are
explain: Similar to the previous logic, shift readings and the final reading are Fore Sights: 5th, 10th, and 15th.

q: 32. The image formed by the objective in the plane of cross hairs is
explain: The objective lens of a surveying telescope forms a real, inverted image of the object in the plane of the cross hairs, which is later magnified (and often re-inverted by additional optics) via the eyepiece.

q: 33. The rise and fall method
options: is less accurate than height of instrument method
is not suitable for leveling with tilting levels
provides a check on the reduction of intermediate point levels
quicker and less tedious for large number of intermediate sights
explain: The key advantage of the rise and fall method over the height of instrument method is that it provides a complete arithmetic check on the reduction of levels for every point, including intermediate sights.

q: 34. If the staff is not held vertical at a leveling station, the reduced level calculated from the observation would be
explain: If the staff is tilted (not held exactly vertical), the recorded staff reading is always greater than the true (minimum) reading, resulting in a calculated reduced level that is more than the true R.L.

q: 35. A straight line tangential to the longitudinal curve of the level tube at its center, is known as
explain: The bubble line (or axis of the level tube) is the tangent to the inner surface of the tube at its midpoint.

q: 36. Collimation method is use in
explain: The height of instrument (collimation) method is commonly applied in both profile leveling and differential leveling operations for reducing levels efficiently.

q: 37. The method of leveling in which the heights of mountains are found by observing temperature at which water boils is known as
explain: Hypsometry (hypometry) is the specific method that determines elevation based on the boiling point of water, which decreases with increasing altitude due to reduced atmospheric pressure.

q: 38. Due to curvature of earth the object
explain: Due to the earth's curvature, a distant object appears to be at a higher position (higher staff reading) than its true elevation would suggest on a flat plane, requiring a subtractive curvature correction.
